Fantasy basketball draft model · H2H points · re-runs for your league in the browser

NBA Fantasy Basketball Points League Database

A projection model you can bend to your own league. Set your scoring and your playoff weeks, switch the optional factors on or off, and both the draft board and 24 seasons of backtest re-rank in front of you.

Your league

Weeks are the fantasy calendar for 2026-27 (24 weeks; the NBA Cup and All-Star weeks are merged). Replacement level is teams × roster spots + 1. Recovery is the share of a missed game you get back from the waiver wire — lower it if your league has few adds or one IR slot. Bonuses stack: with Yes a triple-double also earns the double-double bonus; with No it earns only the highest bonus reached.

Possession load team usage crowding — players on over-stuffed offenses get docked, under-used offenses get a bump; ships to correct a measured bias (roughly neutral on capture). On.
Tank discount −15% on playoff weeks for age-30+ players on bottom-6 Vegas win-total teams — late-season rest and shutdown risk. On.
Experience yr2-4 small development bump for players in NBA years 2–4; the age curve already carries most of it (+0.2pp, p=0.21). Off.
Roster churn flat discount on players who changed teams; failed every test (best p=0.52). Off.
Destination adjusts movers by the scoring their new team must absorb vs their old one; a real effect (p<0.0001) that still costs capture on the board. Off.
Rookies (ESPN proj) seats rookies at their market rank (ESPN’s, consensus fallback) — this model cannot rate players with no NBA minutes. Rows marked RK. On.
Depth minutes nudge where lineups.com’s preseason depth chart disagrees with projected minutes by 8+, the projection blends 25% toward the chart’s slot (30/21/14/10 by string); nudged rows carry a dot on Depth. Six-season test +0.13pp, not significant. On for 2026-27 by the owner’s call — an outlier year of injury returns and team moves.
Games-played weighting how much recent seasons count when projecting games played; 7/2/1 is the shipped setting.
Player evaluation who sets the player order: this model, or the FantasyPros consensus re-scaled by your league’s math (schedule, playoff weeks, replacement).
TANK −15% on playoff weeks — age 30+ on a bottom-6 Vegas team (the only tag that changes value)

Rookie board

This model cannot rank a player with no NBA minutes, so rookies are ranked from every outside pre-draft signal this project holds, side by side: ESPN’s editorial rank, live ADP, the FantasyPros consensus, and — where ESPN publishes a full stat line — the board rank this league’s math implies. All four live on the same overall-rank scale; Rookie rank is their simple average, no fitting.

Read with the base rate in mind: over eight seasons a top-5 pick’s median finish is 101st, and of the rookies ESPN projected top-104 across six backtest seasons, 42% got there (median finish 130). Where Model math is far more bullish than ADP (Boozer, Wilson), that is ESPN’s machine disagreeing with the market — a bet, not a fact. Case-by-case adjustments

Everything above starts from the one formula (Method tab). On top of it sits a documented judgment layer, set player by player from the 2026-09 audits: games rows fix projected games where a draft-day fact (a team-announced surgery timeline, an audited non-injury absence) contradicts trailing history; role rows scale a whole per-game stat line where a role changed in ways the history can’t see (new starters, bench demotions, usage squeezes). Every row carries its working and gets pruned when its reasoning goes stale. Rule-based layers — the depth-chart minutes nudge and the roster corrections — are separate and documented in their own legends.

8-team H2H points · 2026-27 · verified against ESPN league settings

How the board is built

One formula, built up in five stages, then a documented layer of case-by-case judgment on top. Every number below is live from the current board, and one player — Tyrese Maxey — is carried through every stage so you can watch his rank get made.

The whole thing in one line

The formula

A player’s value is the fantasy points he puts on your scoreboard, week by week, across your season. The key idea: when he sits out, you don’t score zero — you pick someone up off waivers. In an 8-team league only 104 players are rostered, so the waiver wire always holds a real NBA starter. A missed game costs you the gap to that player, not the whole game.

for each fantasy week: contribution = games_that_week × leverage × tank_discount × [ availability × fp_per_game + (1 − availability) × recovery × replacement_fp ] value = sum of every week’s contribution vorp = value − value of the 105th-best player → sort by value = the board
1fp_per_game — what he scores in a game he plays
2fp_per_game, adjusted — his team’s context
3availability, recovery, replacement_fp — the games he misses
4games_that_week, leverage, tank_discount — your calendar
5value, vorp — add it up, subtract what’s free, rank

Every control on this page changes one term. Your scoring settings change stage 1, the factor toggles change stage 2, waiver recovery changes stage 3, playoff weeks and weight change stage 4, and teams × roster spots change stage 5. The browser re-runs all five stages for every player whenever you touch anything.

Every parameter was chosen by walk-forward testing: build the board for a past season using only what was knowable before it, then score it against what actually happened. Twenty-four seasons, 1999-00 to 2025-26 — the last one held out of all tuning and spent once, blind, at the end. The Proof tab shows every season.

Stage 1 · fp_per_game

What he scores in a game he plays

Built in two separate pieces, because they behave differently: how productive he is per minute, and how many minutes he plays. Each comes from his last three seasons, with last season counting most. Multiply them and you get a full per-game stat line (points, rebounds, assists, steals, blocks, threes, turnovers…), which is then scored under your settings — including the double-, triple- and quadruple-double bonuses.

MAXEY — stage 1 per-minute production, last three seasons 2023-24 70 gm 37.5 min 43.5 FP per 36 2024-25 52 gm 37.7 min 43.8 FP per 36 2025-26 70 gm 38.0 min 49.7 FP per 36 <- weighted 7x weighted 7 / 2 / 1 ~47.8 FP per 36 age 25 -> still improving x 1.032 minutes, weighted the same way 36.8 per game rate x minutes -> stat line -> your scoring = 50.0 FP/game

How it was derived

Weights 7 / 2 / 1 Last season counts seven times as much as three seasons ago. The textbook weighting (5/4/3) was the worst of every configuration tested; 7/2/1 beat it in every test season on both rank accuracy and value captured. Recent form matters more than the textbook assumes.
Per minute, not per game Across 289 measured in-season trades, a player’s per-minute production did not change when he moved (p = 0.39) — what changed was his minutes. So skill and playing time are projected separately, and a player whose minutes swung isn’t punished for it. Minutes are the single largest source of error in the model, which is why most manual adjustments (below) are minutes calls.
Age curve About +1.6% a year below age 27, −2.4% a year above it. These slopes were doubled in September 2026 after an error audit of 7,011 player-seasons found the gentler curve under-projected players 24 and younger by 2.0 FP/g and over-projected 33+ by 1.5. Doubling won 16 of 23 seasons (+0.43 points of value captured, p = 0.015), with a broad sweet spot from 1.75× to 2.75×. One carve-out: the old-age miss lives entirely in aging role players. Players 33+ still projecting above 35 FP/g were actually under-projected, so they keep the original gentle decline (1.2%/yr).
Rookies No NBA minutes means nothing to project, so rookies are seated at their market rank (ESPN’s, with the expert consensus as fallback) and marked RK. Base rate worth knowing: over eight seasons a top-5 pick’s median finish is 101st — right at replacement level.
Honest limit This is the stage where people beat the model. Over six seasons with a frozen FantasyPros consensus, the experts’ player order captured 2.4 points more value (p = 0.034) — they read camp reports and medical news; box scores can’t. The Player evaluation switch on the Board tab lets the experts set stage 1–2 order while stages 3–5 still apply your league’s math. Walk-forward, that hybrid tied the experts and beat this model by 2.3 points.

Stage 2 · fp_per_game, adjusted

His team’s context

Stage 1 projects every player in the role he held last year. That breaks when a team collects several players who were all the first option somewhere else — there are only so many shots to go around. This stage docks players on over-crowded offenses and bumps players on thin ones.

MAXEY — stage 2 Philadelphia's roster, as projected, would use 136% of the possessions that actually exist (Load column; 1.00 = it adds up) crowding correction for every Sixer -2.0 FP/game 50.0 -> 47.97 FP/game

How it was derived

Possession load The model’s over-projection rises in a straight line with team load — −0.8, +0.7 and +1.4 FP/g across low, middle and high load bands, over 3,249 player-seasons. The size of the correction is fitted to that measured bias (7.09 FP/g per unit of load), learned only from prior seasons. Simply forcing each team’s possessions to add up was also tried: it over-corrects about 2.5× and lost at all four strengths tested.
Depth-chart nudge Where the lineups.com preseason depth chart disagrees with projected minutes by 8 or more, minutes blend 25% toward the chart slot (30 / 21 / 14 / 10 minutes by string). Six-season test: +0.13 points, not significant. On for 2026-27 only by the owner’s call, because this is an outlier year for injury returns and moves; nudged rows carry a dot in the Depth column.
Tried and dropped A discount for changing teams (p = 0.52 — about 38% of players are new or returning every year, so it moves everyone together); a destination-quality adjustment (a real effect, p < 0.0001, that still cost accuracy on the board); a bump for NBA years 2–4 (the age curve already carries it). All three remain as toggles, off by default, so you can see what they would do.

Stage 3 · availability, recovery, replacement_fp

The games he misses

Availability is the share of his team’s games he is expected to play: projected games ÷ 82. For the games he misses, you get partial credit — a recovery share of what a replacement player off waivers would score. Recovery is high in the regular season and low in the fantasy playoffs, when you can’t afford to guess.

MAXEY — stage 3 games played, last three seasons 70 / 52 / 70 -> weighted 66.4 blend: 1/3 his record + 2/3 league average (59.7) (66.4 + 2 x 59.7) / 3 = 62 games availability 62 / 82 = 0.756 a missed game is worth, from waivers: regular season 0.85 x 29.3 FP = 24.9 FP fantasy playoffs 0.35 x 29.3 FP = 10.2 FP

How it was derived

Why blend with league average Games missed last year explain only 11% of games missed next year (r² = 0.11) — mostly noise. So his own record is trusted one-third. The most accurate setting was one-fifth; one-third was chosen deliberately, costing about a tenth of a point of accuracy for roughly 70% more separation between fragile and durable players. It cuts both ways: the fragile lose more, the durable gain more.
Injury type 98,108 injury-report entries were classified by body part to test whether chronic injuries predict future absence better than acute ones. They don’t in any way that improved the board, so the model only counts games missed. Known surgery timelines are handled as manual adjustments instead (below).
Replacement 29.3 FP/g The median scoring rate of the next 16 players past #104 — the realistic waiver pool. A median rather than the single #105 player, because one fragile high-scorer sitting on the boundary once dragged it from ~30 to 37.6 and over-rewarded injury-prone players.
Recovery 0.85 / 0.35 Regular season: how often an absence is known before lineups lock, given unlimited adds (structural range 0.77–0.95). Playoffs: absences bunch up 1.23× in playoff weeks and there’s no time to recover a bad week; walk-forward, raising it cost accuracy (−0.3 points, p = 0.033). Lower the regular-season number if your league limits adds or IR.

Stage 4 · games_that_week, leverage, tank_discount

Your calendar

Everything is priced week by week on the published 2026-27 NBA schedule, so a team with more games in your window is worth more. Only weeks 1–22 count (every team plays 72–74 games in that window). Your playoff weeks, 19–22, count 1.4× because they decide the title. And one narrow group — veterans on teams likely to tank — loses 15% in those playoff weeks.

MAXEY — stages 1-4 put together Philadelphia: 59 regular-season games + 15 in playoff weeks no tank discount (PHI Vegas line 50.5) regular games he PLAYS 59 x 0.756 x 47.97 = 2,139 regular games he MISSES 59 x 0.244 x 0.85 x 29.3 = 359 playoff games he PLAYS 15 x 1.4 x 0.756 x 47.97 = 761 playoff games he MISSES 15 x 1.4 x 0.244 x 0.35 x 29.3 = 53 value = 3,311

How it was derived

Schedule Taken straight from the published fixtures, so it is knowable on draft day — not hindsight. Playoff-week games range from 12 (Cleveland) to 15 across the league: a real but modest 4–6% of value.
Playoff weight 1.4 Started at 2.0. Testing showed the playoff-week schedule barely predicts playoff-week scoring (r = 0.075), so it came down. A sweep from 1.0 to 2.0 across ten seasons was flat (no setting differed by more than 0.16 points), so 1.4 is a stated preference — playoff weeks matter more — that can’t be mis-set enough to hurt.
Tank discount −15% in playoff weeks for players aged 30+ on the bottom fifth of preseason Vegas win totals (currently Sacramento 21.5, Brooklyn 24.5, Milwaukee 25.5, New Orleans 27.5, Memphis and Chicago 29.5 — 11 players flagged TANK). Being on a bad team in general does not cut production — tested against three measures of team quality, every one failed. The effect exists only for veterans on genuinely tanking teams, who kept 80% of their playoff-week minutes versus 95% for younger teammates. Thin evidence (55 veteran-seasons), stated plainly.

Stage 5 · value, vorp

Add it up, subtract what’s free, rank

Eight teams × thirteen roster spots = 104 players rostered, so the 105th-best player is free — he’s on waivers all season. VORP (value over replacement) is how much more a player is worth than him. Players are ranked by value, then grouped into tiers.

MAXEY — stage 5 Maxey's value 3,311 the #105 player's value (free on waivers) - 2,157 VORP 1,154 -> RANK 7

How it was derived

Replacement #105 Straight arithmetic from the verified league settings. This is the single fact that separates this league from the 12-team default public rankings are built for: here replacement is a genuine NBA starter, which is why durable high-floor players rank higher than public boards have them. Checked against daily lineups (only 10 of 13 start each day): across 24 seasons of simulated drafts just 0.6% of drafted players’ points land on the bench, and a starters-only replacement (#81) scored worse on every test — #105 holds.
VORP vs order Subtracting the same number from everyone can’t reshuffle anyone — the order comes from value. VORP tells you what a gap is worth: whether a reach is justified, or how to weigh a trade.
Tiers, not a strict order The board’s rank correlation with real outcomes is about 0.72, and roughly a quarter of picks won’t finish top-105 no matter how good the ranking. It can tell tier 3 from tier 6; it cannot tell pick 31 from pick 34. Inside a tier, draft for fit.
Position scarcity Tested and left out: re-ordering by position moves players an average of 2.3 places and changes who is draftable by nobody.

On top of the formula

Manual adjustments

The formula reads three years of box scores. It cannot see news: a surgery announced in September, a trade, a new starter, a star leaving a team. So on top of it sits a documented judgment layer, set player by player in the September 2026 review of every top-130 player. No formula parameter is ever changed to fit an opinion — judgment lives only in these rows, each with its reasoning written down, and each is deleted when the news resolves.

Games · 24 rows

Replace projected games (stage 3) where a draft-day fact contradicts history: a team-announced surgery timeline (Butler’s ACL → 28 games), or a past absence that wasn’t injury, or an owner durability call.

Role · 50 rows

Scale a player’s whole stat line (stage 1) for a role change history can’t see — set his minutes (Giannis 32, Naz Reid 30 as a new starter) or his per-minute rate (a usage squeeze or a promotion to first option).

Rosters · 6 rows

Trades and signings the NBA’s data hasn’t caught up with yet, so each player is priced on his real team. Removed when the official data catches up — so far every handover has moved players by a place at most.

Injury notes · 20 rows

Display only: the INJ tag and its hover text for players not ready for opening night or carrying real risk. They inform your judgment; they don’t change value.

Every games and role row — what changed, from what to what, and why — is listed in rank order in the Case-by-case adjustments ledger at the foot of the Board tab. Two rules keep the layer honest: a claimed injury is checked against actual games played and the article’s date before it ships (seasonal news gets recycled), and when a check overturns a call, the row changes and the page says so.

Did it work? Twenty-four seasons, rebuilt as if it were draft night

For each season below the board was built using only what was knowable before that season started — three prior years of box scores, the published schedule, the age curve — and then scored against what actually happened, under your scoring system and playoff weighting. Where ESPN’s own pre-draft rank exists it is scored on the identical test, so the comparison is like for like.

ESPN column

ESPN’s published H2H points rankings as they stood before each season, recovered from dated Wayback Machine captures (7 Oct 2024, 3 Oct 2023, 23 Oct 2022, 20 Oct 2021) and, for 2025-26, ESPN’s frozen preseason ranks (verified unrefreshed). The fantasy API’s stored rank for a past season is refreshed during the year and carries hindsight, so it is not used.

A human editor with every roster move, camp report and injury update on the day is a genuinely strong benchmark, and this model reads only box scores and a schedule — read the comparison with that in mind.

FPros column & the hybrid

FPros is the FantasyPros expert consensus for Yahoo points scoring, frozen at each tip-off and verified the same way. It is a multi-expert panel (6–12 experts per season), so a stronger benchmark than any single writer, though built for a different points format.

Experts × your league math re-ranks that consensus with this model’s magnitudes and your schedule, scoring and playoff weighting — the hybrid described on the Method tab.

What gets scored

Projected ranks here come from the base model (projection + schedule + availability + leverage). The optional factors on the Board tab were each tested walk-forward and none was shown to improve this number, so they are not applied to the proof.

The playoff window on this tab uses the league’s default weeks; custom windows apply to the live board.

Seasons left out, and why

2019-20 was suspended in March 2020 and finished in the Orlando bubble with 22 of 30 teams — 63–75 games and no comparable late-season calendar (where your playoff weeks live). 2020-21 was a delayed, compressed 72-game season with heavy COVID-protocol absences. 2011-12 was the 66-game lockout. Scoring a board against those measures the distortion, not the board.

Run as an exhibition anyway (capture self-prorates): 2019-20 board 90.6% vs FantasyPros 93.2%; 2020-21 board 87.1% vs 88.9%. Same direction as the official seasons — excluded for calendar comparability, not because they flatter anyone.

# PlayerTm ProjProj pts ActualActual ptsGP Miss ESPNESPN miss FProsFPros miss

Value captured is the share of the best-attainable points a team would have banked by drafting straight down that ranking to fill every roster in the league. Miss is actual rank minus projected rank: positive means he finished lower than projected. A model that only ever had to beat last year’s totals would sit around 0.87; random drafting sits near 0.60.
